title: Observer, Pub/Sub, Event Bus, Kotlin Flow, and Mediator
scopeHtml: Scope: Observer, pub/sub, event bus, Kotlin Flow and Mediator with refactors, leaks, and when not to use. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Observer: the idea
notes.html:
Observer lets one object (the subject) notify many others (observers) when something changes, without knowing who they are. The subject keeps a list of listeners and calls each when state changes. Observers subscribe and unsubscribe at will.

It removes polling ("did it change yet?") and direct coupling ("when price changes, call chart, call alert, call logger").

+------------------+  1..*  +-------------------+
| Subject          |------->| <<interface>>     |
| - observers      |        | Observer          |
| + subscribe(o)   |        | + onChange(value) |
| + unsubscribe(o) |        +---------+---------+
| + notifyAll()    |                  ^
+------------------+          +-------+--------+
                              |                |
                       PriceChart         AlertService

Before (tight coupling):

class StockTicker {
    private final Chart chart; private final Alerts alerts; private final Logger log;
    void setPrice(double p) {
        chart.draw(p); alerts.check(p); log.write(p);   // knows everyone
    }
}

Adding a fourth consumer means editing StockTicker.

After:

interface PriceObserver { void onPrice(double p); }

class StockTicker {
    private final List<PriceObserver> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    void subscribe(PriceObserver o)   { observers.add(o); }
    void unsubscribe(PriceObserver o) { observers.remove(o); }
    void setPrice(double p) { for (PriceObserver o : observers) o.onPrice(p); }
}
// ticker.subscribe(p -> chart.draw(p));

CopyOnWriteArrayList lets an observer unsubscribe during notification without a ConcurrentModificationException (cost: each add copies the array, fine for few observers).

Kotlin variant.

class StockTicker {
    private val observers = java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList<(Double) -> Unit>()
    fun subscribe(o: (Double) -> Unit) = observers.add(o)
    fun unsubscribe(o: (Double) -> Unit) = observers.remove(o)
    var price: Double = 0.0
        set(v) { field = v; observers.forEach { it(v) } }
}

Decision gravity. Easy to add, but it changes the control flow into something hard to trace ("who reacts to this?"). Adding observers is reversible; letting the whole app depend on implicit notification chains is not (see event storms below).

Everyday analogy. A YouTube channel: you subscribe, the channel does not know your name, new video goes to all subscribers.

Common interview traps.

  • Notifying while holding a lock: an observer that calls back into the subject can deadlock.
  • Not saying whether notifications are synchronous (on the caller's thread) or asynchronous.
  • Order of notification is usually not guaranteed; do not rely on it.

notes.title: Observer in the real world: Android and Java
notes.html:
API Subject Observer
Android View.setOnClickListener View OnClickListener
Android LiveData LiveData<T> Observer<T>, lifecycle-aware
Android BroadcastReceiver system / app receiver (system-wide variant)
Android ContentObserver content provider observer
Jetpack LifecycleOwner Activity/Fragment LifecycleObserver
RxJava Observable Observer / Subscriber
Java PropertyChangeSupport bean PropertyChangeListener
Java Observable/Observer deprecated since Java 9 prefer PropertyChangeListener, Flow, or Rx

Worked example (LiveData). A ViewModel exposes LiveData<List<Order>>. Fragment observes with viewLifecycleOwner. On rotation, the Fragment view is destroyed and the observer is removed automatically; the new view re-subscribes and receives the latest value immediately (replay of 1). No leak, no manual unsubscribe.

viewModel.orders.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { adapter.submitList(it) }

The memory leak (classic incident). A long-lived subject (singleton, Application-scoped) holds a strong reference to a short-lived observer (an Activity). After rotation, the old Activity cannot be garbage collected. Symptom: heap grows 5 to 10 MB per rotation, LeakCanary reports "Activity leaked", eventually OutOfMemoryError. Fix: unsubscribe in onDestroy/onStop, use lifecycle-aware observers, or hold WeakReferences.

Everyday analogy. A group chat notification: everyone in the group gets pinged; leave the group and you stop getting them (forget to leave and your phone buzzes forever).

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the unsubscribe path (lapsed listener problem).
  • Observer on the wrong thread: updating UI from a background thread crashes.
  • Treating LiveData as a general event bus: it replays the last value, so one-shot events (navigate, show toast) fire again after rotation.

notes.title: Pub/sub and the event bus
notes.html:
Publish/subscribe separates the two sides even more: publishers send messages to a topic or channel, subscribers listen to topics, and a broker in between delivers. Neither side holds a reference to the other.

Observer Pub/Sub
Coupling subject knows observers (interface) publisher and subscriber unaware of each other
Middleman none broker / bus
Scope in-process, one object in-process or across machines
Delivery synchronous usually usually async, can be durable

In-process event bus. Android developers know GreenRobot EventBus and Otto (now retired). Pros: very decoupled, tiny API. Cons: hidden control flow, hard to test, hard to find who handles an event, no compile-time guarantee someone listens. Most teams moved to StateFlow/SharedFlow or Rx for typed streams.

Across services. Kafka, RabbitMQ, SNS/SQS, Google Pub/Sub. Different guarantees: Kafka keeps messages on disk by offset (replay, ordered per partition); SNS fans out but each subscriber needs its own queue to be durable.

Worked example. An OrderPlaced event at 500 events/s. Email, inventory and analytics each consume it. If email is down for 10 min, it misses 300,000 events with a plain in-memory bus (lost forever). With Kafka (retention 7 days) it resumes from its committed offset and loses nothing. That durability difference is why in-process bus is not a message queue.

Decision gravity. Introducing an event bus is hard to reverse: once 30 handlers react to OrderPlaced, nobody dares change its shape. Treat event schemas like public APIs (versioned, additive changes only).

Everyday analogy. A radio station: it broadcasts on a frequency; whoever tunes in hears it. The station never knows the listeners.

Common interview traps.

  • Using an event bus when a plain method call is clearer. Hidden flow costs debuggability.
  • Assuming exactly-once delivery. In practice it is at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent.
  • Mixing "event" (a fact that happened) with "command" (a request to do something).

notes.title: Kotlin Flow as a modern Observer
notes.html:
A Kotlin Flow is an observable stream of values over time, built on coroutines. A collector subscribes by calling collect; cancellation unsubscribes automatically when the coroutine dies. Three shapes to know:

Type Hot/cold Replay Typical use
Flow<T> cold: starts per collector none one-off streams (DB query, network)
StateFlow<T> hot latest value, always has one UI state, replaces LiveData
SharedFlow<T> hot configurable (0 default) one-off events, many collectors 
class OrdersViewModel(repo: OrderRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<List<Order>>(emptyList())
    val state: StateFlow<List<Order>> = _state

    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>()       // replay = 0
    val events: SharedFlow<UiEvent> = _events

    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
        _state.value = repo.load()
        _events.emit(UiEvent.Toast("Updated"))
    }
}

// In the Fragment: only collect while at least STARTED
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.state.collect { adapter.submitList(it) }
    }
}

Worked example. StateFlow compares new value with old using equals; setting the same list twice emits once (conflation). A SharedFlow(replay=0) emits to current collectors only, so a toast event is not replayed after rotation (the LiveData bug above). Use SharedFlow or a Channel for one-shot events.

Pitfalls. Collecting in lifecycleScope.launch { } without repeatOnLifecycle keeps collecting in the background (wasted work, crashes touching views). Backpressure: SharedFlow buffer defaults suspend the emitter if a collector is slow; set extraBufferCapacity and onBufferOverflow deliberately.

Decision gravity. Moving from LiveData to StateFlow is a medium, mostly mechanical migration; mixing both in one app is common but doubles concepts.

Everyday analogy. A live scoreboard (StateFlow: always shows the current score) versus a goal announcement over the speakers (SharedFlow: heard only if you were there).

Common interview traps.

  • Explaining StateFlow without mentioning it always has a value and conflates.
  • Collecting a flow with launch only and ignoring lifecycle.
  • Cold vs hot: calling flow {} twice runs the producer twice.

notes.title: Observer refactor: from callbacks to a typed stream
notes.html:
Before (callback hell with manual cleanup):

class Downloader {
    private final List<Listener> listeners = new ArrayList<>();
    interface Listener { void onProgress(int pct); void onDone(File f); void onError(Exception e); }
    void add(Listener l) { listeners.add(l); }
}
// Every screen: implement 3 methods, remember to remove in onDestroy.

After (sealed state + flow):

sealed interface DownloadState {
    data class Progress(val pct: Int) : DownloadState
    data class Done(val file: File) : DownloadState
    data class Error(val cause: Throwable) : DownloadState
}

fun download(url: String): Flow<DownloadState> = flow {
    for (p in 0..100 step 10) { emit(DownloadState.Progress(p)); delay(100) }
    emit(DownloadState.Done(File("a.bin")))
}.catch { emit(DownloadState.Error(it)) }

// Collector gets cleaned automatically on cancel; `when` is exhaustive.

The compiler forces handling all states (when on sealed interface). No remove call; cancellation does it.

When NOT to use Observer.

  • Only one consumer and it is known: call it directly.
  • You need a return value: observers cannot return results to the subject (use Strategy or a function).
  • You need strict ordering or a transaction across consumers: use an explicit orchestrator.
  • High-frequency events (touch move at 120 Hz) with heavy listeners: batch or conflate.

Everyday analogy. Replacing a notebook of "call these three people" with a group broadcast that also keeps the latest status pinned.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing Observer with polling; the point is push, not pull.
  • Loops: A observes B and B observes A, changing state each time = infinite notification loop (a stack overflow in the worst case).

notes.title: Mediator: the idea
notes.html:
Mediator centralises how a set of objects communicate, so they talk to the mediator instead of to each other. With N objects all talking directly, you have up to N(N-1)/2 links (10 objects = 45 links). With a mediator you have N links to the hub.

Before: 5 widgets, each knows others      After: each knows only the mediator
  A--B  A--C  A--D  A--E                     A \
  B--C  B--D  B--E                           B  \
  C--D  C--E   D--E   (10 links)             C ---> [FormMediator]   (5 links)
                                             D  /
                                             E /

Before: a signup form where every widget touches the others.

class CheckBox { Button submit; EditText email; void onChange() { submit.enabled = checked && !email.text.isEmpty(); } }
class EditText { Button submit; CheckBox terms; void onChange() { submit.enabled = !text.isEmpty() && terms.checked; } }

The rule "submit is enabled when email filled and terms checked" is smeared over several classes.

After:

interface FormMediator { void changed(Widget source); }

class SignupMediator implements FormMediator {
    EditText email; CheckBox terms; Button submit;
    public void changed(Widget src) {
        submit.setEnabled(!email.getText().isEmpty() && terms.isChecked());
    }
}
abstract class Widget { protected FormMediator med; void notifyChange() { med.changed(this); } }

Widgets only call med.changed(this). The rule lives in one place and can be tested without any UI.

Kotlin variant.

class SignupMediator {
    var email = ""; var terms = false
    val submitEnabled get() = email.isNotBlank() && terms
}

Real Android: this logic lives in a ViewModel (a mediator between UI widgets and the model), exposing one StateFlow<FormState>.

Real examples.

  • Android ViewModel / MVP Presenter: mediates between View and Model.
  • java.util.Timer coordinates tasks; Swing ButtonGroup.
  • Air traffic control tower: planes talk to the tower, not each other. Chat room server: users post to the room, not to each other.
  • MediatR (.NET) for in-process request/handler dispatch; Spring ApplicationEventPublisher.

Observer vs Mediator. Observer is one-to-many broadcast with no logic ("something changed"). Mediator holds coordination logic ("when A changes, enable B and refresh C"). A mediator is often built with observers underneath.

When NOT to use Mediator.

  • Two or three objects: direct calls are clearer.
  • The mediator grows into a "god object" with 2,000 lines knowing everything. Split by feature or use several small mediators.

Decision gravity. Introducing a mediator is a moderate, local refactor. The cost is hidden: you moved the coupling into the mediator, you did not remove it. Reversible if kept small.

Everyday analogy. Air traffic control: 50 planes never talk to each other, all go through the tower.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling any ViewModel a "Mediator". It is one role of it; say what it coordinates.
  • Describing Mediator as "Observer". Observer broadcasts; Mediator decides.
  • God-object risk not mentioned.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Observer: subject notifies subscribed observers; removes polling and hard-coded callers. Decide sync vs async, and always unsubscribe.
  • Android: LiveData, LifecycleObserver, click listeners. Leaks happen when a long-lived subject keeps a short-lived observer (LeakCanary shows it).
  • Pub/sub adds a broker so neither side knows the other; in-process bus is not durable, Kafka-style brokers are. Handlers must be idempotent (at-least-once).
  • Kotlin Flow: cold Flow, hot StateFlow (state, conflated, always a value), SharedFlow (events). Use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) in UI.
  • Mediator centralises communication among many objects (N links instead of N^2) and holds the coordination rule; ViewModel/Presenter is the Android example. Avoid god-mediators.
  • Do not use these for single known consumers, when a return value is needed, or when strict ordering matters.
